choices.text: Each bond in the polymer is formed stepwise, independently of the other bonds, usually between two difunctional reactants
An initiator adds to a vinyl monomer, and the reactive intermediate adds monomer after monomer in a chain reaction
choices.why: That describes chain-growth polymers (Section 31.1).

choices.text: A strained cycloalkene is opened by a metal catalyst
choices.why: That is ring-opening metathesis polymerization (Section 31.5).

choices.text: A titanium catalyst inserts alkenes into a carbon–metal bond
choices.why: That is Ziegler–Natta polymerization (Section 31.2).

explanation: Step-growth polymers are produced by reactions in which each bond is formed stepwise, independently of the others. Most come from two difunctional reactants, as with nylons and polyesters (Section 21.9), though a single reactant with two different functional groups can also polymerize.

prompt: Nylon 66 is made from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine (1,6-hexanediamine). How many carbon atoms does each of these two monomers contain?
explanation: The section describes Nylon 66 as made from the six-carbon adipic acid and the six-carbon hexamethylenediamine. That is where the name 66 comes from.

choices.text: By polymerizing caprolactam, started by a little water that hydrolyzes some caprolactam to 6-aminohexanoic acid
By reacting adipic acid with hexamethylenediamine
choices.why: That reaction gives Nylon 66, from two difunctional reactants.

choices.text: By reacting diphenyl carbonate with bisphenol A
choices.why: That reaction gives the polycarbonate Lexan.

choices.text: By reacting a diol with a diisocyanate
choices.why: That reaction gives a polyurethane.

explanation: Nylon 6 comes from a single reactant, the six-carbon caprolactam. A small amount of water hydrolyzes some caprolactam to 6-aminohexanoic acid, and nucleophilic addition of the amino group to caprolactam then propagates the polymerization.

prompt: How is a polycarbonate such as Lexan different from a polyester?

choices.text: Its carbonyl group is linked to two –OR groups, O=C(OR)2
Its carbonyl group is linked to one –OR group and one –NR2 group
choices.why: That is a urethane, the linkage in polyurethanes.

choices.text: Its carbonyl group is linked to two –NR2 groups
choices.why: That is a urea.

choices.text: It has no carbonyl group at all
choices.why: Polycarbonates are like polyesters and do contain a carbonyl group, bonded to two –OR groups.

explanation: Polycarbonates are like polyesters, but their carbonyl group is linked to two –OR groups, O=C(OR)2. Lexan, prepared from diphenyl carbonate and bisphenol A, has unusually high impact strength and is used in machinery housings, telephones, bicycle safety helmets, and bulletproof glass.

prompt: What is a urethane functional group?

choices.text: A carbonyl carbon bonded to both an –OR group and an –NR2 group
A carbonyl carbon bonded to two –OR groups
choices.why: That is a carbonate. A urethane has one –OR and one –NR2.

choices.text: A carbonyl carbon bonded to two –NR2 groups
choices.why: That is a urea. A urethane is halfway between a carbonate and a urea.

choices.text: A group with the structure R–N=C=O
choices.why: That is an isocyanate, which reacts with an alcohol to make a urethane.

explanation: A urethane is a carbonyl-containing functional group in which the carbonyl carbon is bonded to both an –OR group and an –NR2 group. It is halfway between a carbonate (two –OR) and a urea (two –NR2).

prompt: What product forms when an alcohol, R′OH, adds to an isocyanate, R–N=C=O?

choices.text: A urethane, RNH–C(=O)–OR′
A urea, RNH–C(=O)–NHR′
choices.why: A urea has two nitrogen groups on the carbonyl carbon. An alcohol supplies an –OR′ group, so the product is a urethane.

choices.text: A carbonate, RO–C(=O)–OR′
choices.why: The isocyanate nitrogen stays in the product, so the carbonyl carbon ends up bonded to one nitrogen and one oxygen group.

choices.text: An amine, RNH2, and carbon dioxide
choices.why: That is what happens when water, not an alcohol, adds to an isocyanate, through a carbamic acid.

explanation: A urethane is typically prepared by nucleophilic addition of an alcohol to an isocyanate. The alcohol oxygen adds to the C=O carbon and the nitrogen picks up hydrogen, giving a carbonyl bonded to –OR′ and –NHR (Exercise 31.4.2). A diol and a diisocyanate react the same way to give a polyurethane.

prompt: In polyurethane synthesis the diol is usually a low-molecular-weight polymer with hydroxyl end-groups. What is its approximate molecular weight, in amu?
explanation: A polyurethane is prepared from a diol and a diisocyanate. The diol is usually a low-molecular-weight polymer (MW ≈ 1000 amu) with hydroxyl end-groups, and the diisocyanate is often toluene-2,4-diisocyanate.

prompt: Why are spandex fibers soft and elastic, while polyurethane insulation foams are rigid?

choices.text: Spandex has a fairly low degree of cross-linking; the foams are made from a polyalcohol, which gives a high amount of three-dimensional cross-linking
Spandex is made from a polyalcohol; the foams are made from a simple diol
choices.why: This is reversed. Foams use a polyalcohol to get extensive cross-linking; spandex has little cross-linking.

choices.text: Spandex is a polyester; the foams are polycarbonates
choices.why: Both are polyurethanes. The difference is the degree of cross-linking.

choices.text: Spandex is highly cross-linked; the foams have no cross-linking at all
choices.why: This is reversed. Low cross-linking makes spandex elastic; high three-dimensional cross-linking makes the foam rigid.

explanation: Polyurethanes for spandex fibers have a fairly low degree of cross-linking, so the polymer is soft and elastic. Polyurethane foams for insulation are generally made with a polyalcohol rather than a diol, so the polymer has a high amount of three-dimensional cross-linking, giving a rigid but very light foam.

prompt: What makes a polyurethane foam when a small amount of water is added during polymerization?

choices.text: Water gives a carbamic acid intermediate that spontaneously loses bubbles of CO2
Water boils off as steam bubbles during the reaction
choices.why: The bubbles come from a chemical reaction: a carbamic acid intermediate loses CO2.

choices.text: Water hydrolyzes the urethane links, releasing hydrogen gas
choices.why: The gas is CO2, from a carbamic acid intermediate, not hydrogen.

choices.text: Water reacts with the diol to release oxygen gas
choices.why: The gas is CO2, from a carbamic acid intermediate, not oxygen.

explanation: Foaming occurs when a small amount of water is added during polymerization, giving a carbamic acid intermediate that spontaneously loses bubbles of CO2 (leaving an amine). The CO2 bubbles make the foam.

prompt: PET is made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid (1,4-benzenedicarboxylic acid). Which is its repeating unit?

choices.text: –O–CH2CH2–O–C(=O)–C6H4–C(=O)–
–O–CH2CH2–O–C(=O)–O–C6H4–O–C(=O)–
choices.why: That has carbonate links, O–C(=O)–O. PET is a polyester: each carbonyl is bonded to one oxygen and one ring carbon.

choices.text: –NH–CH2CH2–NH–C(=O)–C6H4–C(=O)–
choices.why: That is a polyamide. Ethylene glycol supplies –O– links, not –NH– links.

choices.text: –CH2–CH(C6H4CO2H)–
choices.why: That is a chain-growth vinyl polymer unit. PET is a step-growth polyester from a diol and a diacid.

explanation: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) is a polyester. Each –OH of ethylene glycol forms an ester with a –CO2H of terephthalic acid, so the repeating unit is –O–CH2CH2–O–C(=O)–C6H4–C(=O)–, with the C6H4 ring substituted at positions 1 and 4 (Exercise 31.4.1).
